messages.author: 171793e5bd0cb49f
messages.subject: Backref argument in strapply
parts:
Hello, Rists. I have a question about the backref argument of
strapply.

I was working on the "Other applications 5: web crawling / compiling a
web-based corpus" assignment and kept getting this error message:

trying URL 'http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/teaching/
qclwr/web/<a HREF="02.html"'
Error in download.file(current.pages[j], paste(counter, "___",
basename(current.pages[j]), :
cannot open URL 'http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/
teaching/qclwr/web/<a HREF="02.html"'

I narrowed the problem down to this line of code in Stefan's solution:

current.links.1<-unlist(strapply(website, "<a[^<]*?href=\"(?!
#)(?!mailto)(.*?(html?|txt))\"", ignore.case=T, perl=T, backref=-1))

Even though the backref was set to "-1", and therefore only supposed
to return the back-referenced part "(.*?(html?|txt))", it returned the
whole match, beginning with the "<a", as you can see in the URL in the
error message. Out of curiosity I changed the backref argument to "1"
and the script finally worked without problems. If I'm reading
correctly the documentation for strapply ("If negative then only the
that number of backreferences are passed but the match itself is
not.") the backref argument "-1" should have given me the correct
links. Am I reading something wrong? I assume strapply doesn't work
differently on a Mac, right? I fixed the problem, so this post is more
for my understanding of strapply. (I, too, am looking forward to
strapplyc, by the way.)

Thanks for all your collective R wisdom. Earl Brown

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Backref argument in strapply
parts: Hm, yes, as you wrote

"Even though the backref was set to "-1", and therefore only supposed
to return the back-referenced part "(.*?(html?|txt))", it returned the

whole match [...]" I am getting the same problem here, and backref=1
does the job.

Off the top of my head, that is kinda confusing so I tried this:

#########################
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(gsubfn)
qwe <- c("abcdef", "ghijkl", "mbcdef")

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If zero or positive the match is passed as the first argument to the
replacement function followed by the indicated number of
backreferences as subsequent arguments.
strapply(qwe, "(.)b", perl=TRUE, backref=1)
[[1]]
[1] "a"

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "m"


# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If negative then only the that number of backreferences are passed
but the match itself is not.

strapply(qwe, "(.)b", perl=TRUE, backref=-1)
[[1]]
[1] "ab"

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "mb"
#########################

The output doesn't seem to be what one would expect. And here is a
maybe more confusing example from strapply's help page:

#########################
# running window of 5 characters using 0-lookahead perl regexp
# Note that the three ( in the regexp will fool it into thinking there
# are three backreferences so specify backref explicitly.
x <- "abcdefghijkl"

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If negative then only the that number of backreferences are passed
but the match itself is not.

# THIS! is the code Gabor provides, but probably not the result he intended?
strapply(x, "(.)(?=(....))", paste0, backref = -2, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
[1] "aabcde" "bbcdef" "ccdefg" "ddefgh" "eefghi" "ffghij" "gghijk" "hhijkl"

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If zero or positive the match is passed as the first argument to the
replacement function followed by the indicated number of
backreferences as subsequent arguments.
# THIS! is not the code Gabor provides, but probably the result he intended?
strapply(x, "(.)(?=(....))", paste0, backref = 2, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
[1] "abcde" "bcdef" "cdefg" "defgh" "efghi" "fghij" "ghijk" "hijkl"
#########################

Weird ...

Re the assignment script: One can of course use this:

sub("^.*?\"", "",
exact.matches("<a[^<]*?href=\"(?!#)(?!mailto).*?(html?|txt)(?=\")",
website, case.sens=FALSE)[[1]], perl=TRUE)

Still, the strapply approach is nicer but right now - it's late here -
I don't see the logic esp. in the example from the website itself ...

STG

messages.author: 171793e5bd0cb49f
messages.subject: Re: Backref argument in strapply
parts:
Apparently, the tcl engine and the R engine treat the backref argument
differently, as switching the perl argument seems to switch the
polarity of the backref argument. Gabor says in this post
http://groups.google.com/group/corpling-with-r/browse_thread/thread/d30502e17afee11f
that: "Using perl = TRUE will cause strapply to use the slower R
engine whereas by default strapply uses faster tcl engine (if you
don't specify perl and if you have tcltk installed)."

Thus, I get the one result, the same result, if I use

perl=FALSE, backref=-1
or
perl=TRUE, backref=1

and a different result if I use

perl=TRUE, backref=-1
or
perl=FALSE, backref=1

Here's a simple example to illustrate:

> text<-"Some sentence whatever it may be."

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=FALSE, backref=-1))
[1] "whatever"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=TRUE, backref=1))
[1] "whatever"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=TRUE, backref=-1))
[1] "sentence whatever it"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=FALSE, backref=1))
[1] "sentence whatever it"

I don't know what engines are (tcl versus R engine) but it appears
that the problem might have to do with the engine that strapply uses.

Thanks for the exact.matches()[[1]] plus gsub() work-around. Earl Brown

Thanks for finding and investigating this. Its supposed to process
the match plus the back references if backref >= 0 and only the back
references otherwise. Thus the "tcl" engine seems to be working as
expected but the "R" engine has it backwards. I have just committed a
fix to the development version so the corrected version can be fetched
from there like this:

> library(gsubfn)
Loading required package: proto
> source("http://gsubfn.googlecode.com/svn-history/r81/trunk/R/gsubfn.R")
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = -1, engine = "R")
[1] "b/c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = 1, engine = "R")
[1] "ab b/ac c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = -1)
Loading required package: tcltk
Loading Tcl/Tk interface ... done
[1] "b/c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = 1)
[1] "ab b/ac c"
